name: Python
summary: Build confidence with core Python, collections, files, JSON, and the standard library.

lessons.title: Values, names, and output
lessons.explanation: Assign a name with =. Python determines the type of the value at runtime. A string, integer, float, and Boolean are distinct kinds of values. An f-string inserts values between braces and can format numbers.
lessons.example:
items = 3
price = 2.75
discounted = False
print(f"{items} items cost ${items * price:.2f}")
print(type(discounted).__name__)

api.name: print(value)
api.description: Write values to the console.

api.name: int(text) / float(text)
api.description: Convert valid numeric text. Conversion can raise ValueError.

api.name: type(value)
api.description: Inspect the runtime type of a value.

lessons.practice: Change the quantity and price. Predict the formatted output before you run it.
lessons.pitfall: Adding a string to an integer raises TypeError. Convert deliberately or use an f-string.

exercise.expected: Print an item count and a total formatted to two decimal places.
exercise.completion: The result ends with two decimal digits for an integer-valued total too.

lessons.title: Conditions, loops, and ranges
lessons.explanation: A colon ends the header. In the multiline form, an indented body follows. Use if, elif, and else for alternatives. A for loop takes successive values from an iterable. A while loop repeats while its condition holds.

api.name: range(start, stop, step)
api.description: Generate integer positions without allocating a list. The stop value is excluded.

api.name: enumerate(items, start=0)
api.description: Produce an index and value for each item.

api.name: zip(a, b)
api.description: Pair values from both iterables, stopping at the shorter one by default.

lessons.practice: Read a nonnegative upper bound from stdin. Print multiples of 3 down to 1 in descending order.
lessons.pitfall: Keep indentation consistent. A misplaced indent changes which block executes.

exercise.expected: Print each multiple on a separate line and no lines when there are no multiples.
exercise.completion: Try an exact multiple, a value between multiples, and a bound below 3.

lessons.title: Lists, dictionaries, sets, and tuples
lessons.explanation: Use a list for a sequence you need to change, a tuple for a fixed sequence, a dictionary for key-to-value lookups, and a set for membership and uniqueness. Lists and tuples are indexed from zero.

api.name: list.append(item)
api.description: Append one item in place.

api.name: dict.get(key, default)
api.description: Read a key or return the fallback.

api.name: set.add(item)
api.description: Include an item once.

api.name: sorted(iterable)
api.description: Return a new sorted list without changing the input.

lessons.practice: Count the first letters of several words. Use a set to show how many distinct letters appear.
lessons.pitfall: list.sort() modifies the list and returns None. Use sorted() when you need a new list.

exercise.expected: Count each word in a list and report unique words in sorted order.
exercise.completion: Repeated words increment their count and empty input produces an empty result.

lessons.title: Functions, comprehensions, and modules
lessons.explanation: Use def to name a reusable operation and return to send back a result. Comprehensions combine a transform and an optional filter. Import standard modules by name to reuse their functions.
lessons.example:
from math import sqrt

def small_roots(values, limit=20):
    return [sqrt(value) for value in values if 0 <= value <= limit]

print(small_roots([4, 9, 25, -1]))

api.name: math.sqrt(value)
api.description: Return the square root of a non-negative value.

api.name: sum(items)
api.description: Add numeric values from an iterable.

api.name: any(items) / all(items)
api.description: Test whether at least one item or every item is truthy.

lessons.practice: Write a function that returns the lengths of words longer than a threshold.
lessons.pitfall: Avoid a list or dictionary as a default parameter when callers need independent values. Defaults are evaluated once.

exercise.expected: Return the square roots of nonnegative values under an adjustable limit.
exercise.completion: Inputs above the limit and negative inputs are excluded.

lessons.title: Classes and dataclasses
lessons.explanation: A class keeps related state and operations together. Instance methods receive the current object through self. A dataclass can generate the initializer and useful comparison and display methods from its declared fields.

api.name: @dataclass
api.description: Generate common methods from annotated fields.

api.name: isinstance(value, Class)
api.description: Test whether a value belongs to a class or one of its subclasses.

lessons.practice: Add a quantity field and a total_cents method to Receipt.
lessons.pitfall: Type hints help readers and tools. Ordinary Python execution does not enforce them.

exercise.expected: Model a study session with a dataclass and print a readable summary.
exercise.completion: Two instances can store different durations without sharing state.

lessons.title: Exceptions and validation
lessons.explanation: Wrap an operation that may fail in try, then catch specific error types with except. Validate values at the boundary and use raise when a function cannot produce a meaningful result.

api.name: ValueError
api.description: Report a valid type that carries an unacceptable value.

api.name: FileNotFoundError
api.description: Report an attempted file access where the path is missing.

api.name: finally
api.description: Run cleanup after a try block, including when an exception occurs.

lessons.practice: Extend positive_count to reject counts above 100. Try 0, 1, 100, 101, and invalid text.
lessons.pitfall: Keep the try block narrow so a genuine bug elsewhere does not look like a user input error.

exercise.expected: Validate a count from text with a clear error for malformed or nonpositive values.
exercise.completion: Handle valid input, nonnumeric text, zero, and a negative count.

lessons.title: Files, paths, and JSON
lessons.explanation: pathlib represents paths as values you can compose. JSON converts simple data to text for storage or exchange. Choose an encoding and validate decoded data before relying on it.
lessons.example:
import json
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "scores.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps({"scores": [8, 9]}), encoding="utf-8")
    saved = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(sum(saved["scores"]))

api.name: Path.read_text() / Path.write_text()
api.description: Read or write the contents of a small text file.

api.name: json.dumps() / json.loads()
api.description: Encode a value to JSON text or decode JSON text.

api.name: with path.open(...) as file
api.description: Open a file and close it automatically when the block ends.

lessons.practice: Save two named scores and calculate the average after reading the data back.
lessons.pitfall: JSON decoding can fail, and valid JSON can have an unexpected shape. Check both.

exercise.expected: Save and load a dictionary containing a list of scores.
exercise.completion: Verify the score total after reloading and check the behavior of malformed JSON.

lessons.title: Counters, statistics, and assertions
lessons.explanation: Reuse tested tools for common operations. Counter tallies repeated values, statistics handles descriptive calculations, and a small assertion can make an example self-checking.
lessons.example:
from collections import Counter
from statistics import mean

readings = [12, 15, 15, 18]
counts = Counter(readings)
print(counts.most_common(1))
assert mean(readings) == 15

api.name: collections.Counter(items)
api.description: Count hashable values.

api.name: statistics.mean(values)
api.description: Compute the arithmetic mean of nonempty data.

api.name: unittest.TestCase.assertEqual(a, b)
api.description: Compare two values in a repeatable unit test.

lessons.practice: Add an outlier and compare statistics.mean with statistics.median.
lessons.pitfall: Use explicit validation for real inputs. Python can omit assert statements when optimization is enabled.

exercise.expected: Find the most common reading and compare it with the mean.
exercise.completion: Use a list whose mode differs from its mean and explain each number.

lessons.title: Avoid shared mutable default arguments
lessons.explanation: Python evaluates a default argument expression when the function is defined. A list used as that default can therefore carry changes from one call to the next. Use None to request a fresh list, then construct it inside the function.
lessons.example:
def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    if tags is None:
        tags = []
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

print(add_tag("math"))
print(add_tag("art"))

api.name: is None
api.description: Check whether the caller requested the default state.

api.name: list.append()
api.description: Change the current list in place.

lessons.practice: Write a function that appends a study result to an optional caller-provided list.
lessons.pitfall: Checking if not tags would also replace a deliberately supplied empty list.

exercise.expected: Calls without a list each receive a fresh one. A supplied empty list receives the new result.
exercise.completion: Compare two default calls and one call with an explicit empty list.

lessons.title: Generate values lazily with yield
lessons.explanation: Calling a generator function creates an iterator. The body starts when iteration asks for a value and pauses at each yield. This lets you process values one at a time without constructing a complete output list.

api.name: yield
api.description: Return one item to the caller and suspend the generator.

api.name: next(iterator)
api.description: Advance the iterator, or raise StopIteration if it is exhausted.

lessons.practice: Yield each cleaned nonblank line from an iterable of text lines.
lessons.pitfall: An iterator can be consumed. A second loop over the same exhausted generator produces no values.

exercise.expected: The result drops blank lines and strips surrounding whitespace.
exercise.completion: Read one item with next, then consume the rest and verify that the first item does not appear again.

lessons.title: Use context managers for deterministic cleanup
lessons.explanation: A with statement asks a context manager to set up a resource and handle exit from the block. File objects close at exit even if the body raises an exception. Opening a text file with an explicit encoding avoids depending on the machine’s default.
lessons.example:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "notes.txt"
    path.write_text("ion", encoding="utf-8")
    with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as stream:
        print(stream.read())
    print("closed:", stream.closed)

api.name: Path.open()
api.description: Open a file from a pathlib path.

api.name: with resource as name
api.description: Bind the managed object within a block and run exit handling afterward.

lessons.practice: Read the first line of a temporary file, then raise an example exception inside the with block.
lessons.pitfall: The name can still refer to the file object after the block, but the file is already closed.

exercise.expected: Handle the expected exception outside the with block and verify the resource is closed.
exercise.completion: Run the normal path and the exception path, using a temporary file each time.

lessons.title: Sort structured data with keys and tie-breakers
lessons.explanation: sorted returns a new list and accepts a function that extracts a comparison key. A tuple key compares its first element, then later elements as needed. Python’s sort is stable, so equal keys retain their original order.
lessons.example:
rows = [("Zoe", 8), ("Ada", 8), ("Sam", 10)]
ranking = sorted(rows, key=lambda row: (-row[1], row[0]))
for name, score in ranking:
    print(f"{name}: {score}")

api.name: sorted(iterable, key=...)
api.description: Create a sorted list using a key function.

api.name: tuple key
api.description: Compare several ordering keys in sequence.

lessons.practice: Rank sessions by descending minutes and then ascending activity name.
lessons.pitfall: reverse=True reverses every part of the ordering, including the tie-breaker. Negate a numeric key when only that key should descend.

exercise.expected: Activities with equal minutes are ordered by name and the input stays unchanged.
exercise.completion: Use duplicate durations, an empty input, and a negative test value if your data policy allows it.

lessons.title: Validate typed data at runtime
lessons.explanation: Type hints help a checker and readers understand intended shapes. They do not validate the result of json.loads. At a boundary, check the actual value before building a typed result. Python bool is a subclass of int, so the check below requires the exact built-in int type for minutes.

api.name: TypedDict
api.description: Describe the field types of a dictionary for a type checker.

api.name: isinstance()
api.description: Check an object against a class or accepted set of classes at runtime.

lessons.practice: Extend the input validator with a required day field and report the invalid field in each error.
lessons.pitfall: An annotation alone will not stop a JSON Boolean or string from reaching your function.

exercise.expected: Return a validated record with precise errors for missing fields and incorrect types.
exercise.completion: Include true, a numeric string, and a negative number for minutes.

lessons.title: Read quoted CSV rows safely
lessons.explanation: A CSV parser understands quoting and separators inside quoted fields. DictReader maps each row to its header names. When opening a real CSV file for this module, pass newline="" so the parser can handle line endings correctly.
lessons.example:
import csv
from io import StringIO

source = StringIO('activity,minutes\n"read, review",25\npractice,10\n')
rows = list(csv.DictReader(source))
for row in rows:
    print(row["activity"], int(row["minutes"]))

api.name: csv.DictReader()
api.description: Yield dictionaries whose keys come from the CSV header by default.

api.name: StringIO
api.description: Provide an in-memory text stream for a reproducible local example.

lessons.practice: Group total minutes by activity from a CSV file.
lessons.pitfall: Splitting text on commas breaks a quoted field that contains a comma.

exercise.expected: Quoted commas stay inside the activity name and a malformed duration is reported with its row number.
exercise.completion: Try quoted text, repeated activities, and a missing duration.

lessons.title: Use the standard library to test behavior
lessons.explanation: A unittest.TestCase groups named test methods. Test an expected value and a rejected input independently, so a change that breaks either behavior is easy to diagnose. A test suite can run with the standard library, with no external dependency.
lessons.example:
import unittest

def duration(raw):
    value = int(raw)
    if value < 0:
        raise ValueError("negative minutes")
    return value

class DurationTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_zero(self):
        self.assertEqual(duration("0"), 0)

    def test_negative(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            duration("-1")

tests = unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(DurationTests)
result = unittest.TestResult()
tests.run(result)
print(f"{result.testsRun} tests passed" if result.wasSuccessful() else "failure")
raise SystemExit(0 if result.wasSuccessful() else 1)

api.name: assertEqual()
api.description: Compare the actual and expected values with a useful failure message.

api.name: assertRaises()
api.description: Require an exception of the expected type from the enclosed behavior.

lessons.practice: Add tests for malformed text and an ordinary positive value.
lessons.pitfall: Testing only the successful input leaves error handling unprotected.

exercise.expected: The suite covers success and rejection and returns an unsuccessful status when a test fails.
exercise.completion: Deliberately change one expected value, observe failure, and then restore it.

prerequisites: Know how to save a source file.
Use Python 3.11 or newer. Examples use the standard library and need no packages.
metadata.miniProject: Build a local study-log report. Read a CSV file with names and minutes, reject malformed rows, and group totals by activity. Add tests for quoted fields, empty input, and a malformed duration.
